en: A Brief Commentary on the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom: A Record for Clarifying the Correct (Volume One).
*The Record for Clarifying the Correct: A Commentary on the Heart Sūtra of Prajñā* (Including Preface), composed by the Śramaṇa Zhongxi of Jin Yun.
I have previously composed a sub-commentary on the Great Master Xianshou’s *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra-śāstra*, annotating it beneath the sūtra text and arranging its topical outline;

I have also written one fascicle of explanatory notes, titled *Xianzheng Wenhua* (Manifesting the Correct Text and Refining the Language), which I intended merely to prevent students from neglecting or forgetting [the teachings].
How could I dare to present this to the enlightened predecessors? Thus it was said during the era of the Great Song.
Preface, written on the first day of the last month of winter in the fourth year of the Qingli era, the year of Jia Shen.
A Brief Commentary on the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom (with Preface).

The explanation of the commentary is divided into two parts. First, the title. Second, the ten characters of the general title of the sutra and its commentary consist of three layers of subject and object:

the two characters "Brief Commentary" (*piěshù*) constitute the subject (the means of explanation), while the remainder constitute the object (that which is explained). The character "Sutra" (*jīng*) is the subject (the means of expression), and everything above it is the object (that which is expressed).
The character "Mind" (*xīn*) is the subject (the metaphor), and everything above it is the object (that which is metaphorized). Now, we take the title of the sutra as a whole.
"Sū" (Commentary) is a specific name for a commentary, while "Sū" itself is the general term.

Regarding the commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, it is designated by the term "Prajñā" and so forth according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound, as explained below in the introductory section.

As for the term "Brief Commentary" (*Lüshù*), it means that this commentary merely explains the general purport of the sūtra text and does not further elaborate upon the names and essences of various dharmas, such as the three categories of objects and wisdom.
Therefore, it is called "abridged" (*lue*). Furthermore, because it simplifies what is not an extensive commentary but instead explains only the abridged root text, it is also termed "abridged.

As for "commentary" (*shu*), it means "to loosen" (*shu*) and "to decide" (*jue*). Because it loosens and connects the textual passages while deciding and selecting their meanings and purports, it is called a "commentary.
Regarding "along with the preface," this indicates that this commentary is accompanied by a preface.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Fazang, who translated the scriptures.

Regarding the second point, as for the title "Śramaṇa who translated the scriptures" and so forth: because the author of the commentary had previously participated in the translation assemblies and was fully engaged in the translation of sutras and śāstras, he is referred to here simply as a "translator of scriptures" (*fan jing*) out of respect for his preeminent achievements and for the sake of brevity. "Śramaṇa" refers to a son of the Śākya [Buddha].
The general title *śramaṇa* in the Sanskrit language is translated here as "diligent and quiescent.

This refers to one who is able to diligently cultivate the precepts, meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), thereby extinguishing delusions, karma, and suffering; thus, it is a general designation for one who gives rise to the wholesome and extinguishes the unwholesome.
"Fazang" (Fa-tsang) is the personal name of the author of this commentary; he was originally from the country of Kang, surnamed Kang, and resided in Xitai during his ordinary life.
The third patriarch of the Huayan school at Yuan Temple established five types of teachings to judge the holy words of the Tathāgata throughout his entire life;

there was no principle that these did not exhaustively encompass. Subsequent generations composed their works with a reverence that dared not fail to follow them, resulting in numerous writings that circulate to this day, their fame shaking the age and their radiance illuminating ten thousand ages.
He was posthumously granted the title of Great Master Xianshou, as detailed in his separate biography.
The statement that he "expounds" rather than "creates" is also a humble expression; thus, the *Lunyu* says, "I expound but do not create;
I trust in and love antiquity," and so forth.
Now, as for the True Source and the Primordial Model, their profound stillness is separated from the fish-trap and rabbit snare [of words].
The second part, the commentary on the text, has three sections: first, a general summary of the main intent; second, an extensive exposition of the scriptural text;

and third, a specific analysis of difficult passages. Regarding the first [the general summary], there are three aspects of Prajñā: first, the *lakṣaṇa* (real mark), which is the essence of the principle to be contemplated; second, the *vipaśyanā* (contemplative illumination), which is the function of the wisdom that contemplates;

and third, the *vyañjana* (letters/words), which is the teaching that explains the former two. The reason for providing this full exposition here is that the subsequent commentary as a whole relies upon these three.
The third [section] concerns the fundamental purpose (*abhiprāya*); thus, the text is divided into two parts. First, the exposition of that which is expressed (*vācya*).

This consists of four sections: first, the object and wisdom are beyond verbal expression; however, within this text, each of these—object and wisdom—has four meanings: (1) the direct indication of their essence (*svabhāva*), (2) the praise of the qualities of their essence, (3) the manifestation of the measure of their essence, and (4) the demonstration that the essence is free from faults.
Upon entering the text, one sees it divided into two parts. First, the clarification of the objective realm of principle (*tattva-viṣaya*). Now, as for "the... [the following ensues].

The opening of this discourse begins with the two characters "zhényuán" (true source). These two words specifically and directly point to the *prajñā-pāramitā* of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) as the essential principle that serves as the object of contemplation.
"True" (*zhēn*) means reality; "source" (*yuán*) is used metaphorically because this true mark is fundamentally not false or deceptive.
Therefore, it is called "true. As the sutra below states: "Therefore, within emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness..."
The meaning of "following conditions" (suiyuan) is illustrated by the metaphor of a water source that can branch into ten thousand streams; the *Xiajing* further states, "emptiness is itself form.
Regarding the term "pure model" (sufan): because this principle-substance cannot be defiled by delusions, it is called "pure" (*su*), which signifies cleanliness.

Because it serves as a model that gives rise to sentient beings' understanding and maintains its own nature, it is called a "model" (*fan*), which signifies a dharma. A dharma takes "providing a model" and "maintaining" as its essential meaning.
Therefore, this praises the virtue of the essence of principle (*tattva*). "Profound and vast" (*chōng-mok*): "profound" (*chōng*) means deep; "vast" (*mok*) refers to the desert.
This means that the essence of principle vertically exhausts the three periods of time, hence it is called "profound. The *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué shū*) states:

"The past has no beginning and the future has no end; horizontally it pervades the ten directions. It is metaphorically compared to the desert because its breadth is boundless. Furthermore, the *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* says: [omitted].

"To say that one exhausts the ten directions and finds no limit" reveals the magnitude of the essence of reality (*dharmatā*). The following passage shows that this essence of reality is free from faults;
thus it says, "separated from the *quán* (fish-trap) and *dì* (rabbit-net). "Separated" (*gé*) means "cut off" (*jué*). A *quán* is used to catch fish, and a *dì* is used to net rabbits;
therefore, the *Zhou Yi* states: "Having obtained the rabbit, forget the net; having obtained the fish, forget the trap. Here, the terms "trap" and "net" are borrowed for illustrative purposes.

The analogy of the fish and the rabbit illustrates the relationship between words and the principle they signify. One who perceives the True Reality must forget the verbal teachings, just as one who has obtained the fish or the rabbit must forget the trap or the snare.
Although the True Reality is provisionally manifested through written words, the essence of the True Reality is fundamentally not words.
As the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa Sūtra* states: "The wondrous nature is perfectly luminous, transcending all names and marks. *Pān* (般) [is a scribal error for *pán* (槃)].
If a sutra states that "dhāraṇī is not words, yet words manifest dhāraṇī," it is because its essence transcends words;
thus, it is said to be separated from the "trap" (the means).
The profound path of wondrous awakening is so deep and subtle that it surpasses both speech and form.

The two characters "Miaojue" (Wondrous Enlightenment) below clarify the wondrous nature of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). The two characters "Miaojue" specifically refer to the *prajñā* of contemplation as the essence of the subject that contemplates.
"Wondrous" (*miao*) refers to that which is inconceivable; "enlightenment" (*jue*) is precisely illumination. Because this essence of wisdom cannot be reached by thought, it is called "wondrous.
As the Sutra below states: "Practicing the profound *prajñā-pāramitā*," etc., it is a spiritual luminosity that reflects and illuminates.
Therefore it is said: "Awakening. The subsequent passage states that Prajñā takes divine discernment as its essence; this refers to the profound principle (*xuanyou*).
Here, "profound" (*xuan*) means mysterious and deep, while "principle" (*you*) means the Way (*dao*). This collectively indicates that the essence of this wisdom is the most ultimate, profound Way.
However, the Way has two meanings: first, the meaning of cause; for the immeasurable fruits of virtue cannot be realized without wisdom.
Second, regarding the meaning of "penetration" (*tong*): since it begins with ordinary beings and all reach the ultimate fruit by means of this wisdom, it is collectively termed "profound" (*you*).
This praises the virtue of the essence of wisdom. As for "mysterious and abstruse" (*aoze*), it refers to the sense of vertical depth;

because it reveals that this is not the shallow wisdom of the provisional or the Lesser Vehicle, it is called "mysterious and abstruse. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The great ocean of the Prajñāpāramitā is exhausted only by the Buddha."
The subsequent text states: "To describe the profound practice of Prajñāpāramitā as 'profound and subtle' (àozé) is indeed appropriate, for it encompasses the vertical within the horizontal;
thus, only 'profound and subtle' is indicated here, which reveals the magnitude of the essence of wisdom (*jñāna*).

The *Kanding ji* explains that because *prajñā* (discernment) is capable of selecting and rejecting, it exists during the causal stage, whereas *jñāna* (realization) merely involves decisive judgment and resides only at the stage of fruition. Here, however, *prajñā* is identical to *jñāna*."
It may be analyzed as follows: because the essence of wisdom (*jñāna-svabhāva*) is free from error, it is said to "transcend words and images.

"Words" refers to speech; "images" refers to conceptual representations. These correspond to their respective meanings. Now, both language and the characteristics of meaning arise from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*);

since the essence of this contemplative wisdom is not conceptual discrimination, it transcends words and images. Furthermore, the *Zhou Yi* states: "When one attains the image, one forgets the words."
When one attains the meaning, one forgets the symbols.
Although both the ultimate and the conventional are simultaneously extinguished, the two truths constantly persist.

Although the ultimate and the inferior [conventional] are clearly distinguished, the essence of object and wisdom is neither two nor three. First, there is a separate clarification of the non-duality of object and wisdom; second...

First, it clarifies that the objective realm is non-dual; however, this objective realm of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) being contemplated is neither real nor conventional, yet it is both real and conventional.

Thus, the two truths are simultaneously present and simultaneously extinguished, such that presence and extinction are non-dual. When it is said that "the real and the conventional are both dissolved," "dissolved" means extinguished.

The "real" refers to the truth of reality (*paramārtha-satya*), which is a single essence without distinction; the "conventional" refers to the truth of convention (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which comprises the myriad phenomena.

There is a difference from the present [view] because when the ultimate (paramārtha-satya) is realized as being identical to the conventional (saṃvṛti-satya), the ultimate perishes; and because when the conventional is realized as being identical to the ultimate, the conventional perishes.

Since they mutually negate one another and both perish, this is called "the simultaneous sublation" (shuang-min). Regarding the phrase "the two truths constantly exist" (*heng-cun*): "existence" means that because the conventional is identical to the ultimate, the ultimate exists;

and because the ultimate is identical to the conventional, the conventional exists. Since they thus mutually perish yet mutually exist, it is said they "constantly exist," meaning they are eternally so.
As clarified above, because it is manifest yet hidden, both [manifestation and concealment] are extinguished; because it is hidden yet manifest, it eternally persists.
Since concealment and manifestation are simultaneous, there is only the single reality-mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of *prajñā* as the object of contemplation—is this not wondrous?

The Sūtra section explains emptiness separately according to the capacities of sentient beings; therefore, the subsequent text says, "illumining the emptiness of the five aggregates," and further says, "all dharmas."

Within the great section on the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*), it is universally stated that [all phenomena] are pure and so forth; yet if one discusses the underlying principle of its general intent, they are in fact eternally perfect.

As the text below states: "Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form," and so on. For this reason, when the Master of the Commentary (the *Sūtra-śāstra-kāra*) later judges this to be subsumed under the Real Teaching (*samyag-naya*), the essential point of his intention lies therein.
When both emptiness and existence are simultaneously transcended, the single flavor is eternally manifest.

When emptiness and existence are below [the level of conceptualization], the wisdom of non-duality clearly perceives that the object of contemplation—being neither existent nor non-existent—already exists;

thus, the wisdom that contemplates as non-dual is also hidden and revealed at the same time. The analogy of the "box and its lid" (*hángài*) may serve to illustrate this principle regarding emptiness, existence, and so forth.

That which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the illumination of the ultimate truth; this is the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*). That which is existence (*bhāva*) is the illumination of the conventional; this is the wisdom of measure (*pramāṇa-jñāna*).
When the true object is signless, the wisdom that illuminates it is called "emptiness"; when the conventional object has myriad distinctions, the wisdom that contemplates it is termed "existence.

Now, because emptiness is identical to existence, emptiness vanishes; because existence is identical to emptiness, existence vanishes. Thus it is said that both are "lost"—this refers to the vanishing of both. This is the text concerning this wisdom.

That which is "merely lost and no longer existing" is clearly indicated in the preceding text. Regarding the phrase "of one flavor," etc., this is a summary concluding that existence and non-existence are non-dual;
because the essence of the wisdom of contemplative observation (*prajñā*) alone is the capacity for observation and is not subject to arising or ceasing, it is said to be "constantly manifest."
It is because true emptiness has never been non-existent; by means of existence, one distinguishes emptiness from illusion. It is because illusory existence has never begun as non-empty;
by means of emptiness, one clarifies existence.

It is precisely because of this that the following two [sections] provide a comprehensive explanation of why they are non-dual. Some say that "object" and "wisdom" each constitute a duality, hence the name.
The meanings differ significantly; how is it that here they are both said to be non-dual? I shall now explain this in detail so that you may understand the reason.
Regarding the phrase "It is truly because," "truly" (良) means "in fact," and "because" (以) means "due to the fact that.

The intended meaning is that the previous statement—that the ultimate and conventional truths are non-dual—is actually due to the fact that the emptiness of the ultimate truth constantly follows conditions to form the existence of the conventional truth, without ever being interrupted.

Regarding the phrase "because it is severed, it is said that there has never been anything that is not existence," and so forth: since the entirety of emptiness constitutes existence, one conversely understands that existence is itself true emptiness.
Therefore, as previously stated, the conventional is identical to the ultimate; thus, by saying "identical to existence," one distinguishes it from emptiness.
Regarding "illusory existence" and so forth: the initial [state] is likewise as it was before. The existence of the conventional truth arises from conditions and lacks intrinsic nature. It is...

Because true emptiness (*tattva-śūnyatā*) has never possessed substantial reality, it is said that "from the very beginning there was nothing that was not empty," and thus "emptiness itself" and so forth.

Since all existence is entirely emptiness, one conversely understands that emptiness is itself illusory existence. Therefore, because it was previously stated that "the ultimate is itself the conventional," it is said "emptiness itself" to clarify the nature of existence.
Since the object of contemplation is such that the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual, there is only a single reality.

How could the wisdom that is able to contemplate the marks be of a different path? One should reflect upon this by taking the object as the standard; there is no need for an elaborate explanation. Question:
Previously, you clarified non-duality, yet now you distinguish between the object and the wisdom. What is the reason for not distinguishing them here? Answer:

Because the essence is itself the function, the principle is not separate from the wisdom-function. Because the function is itself the essence, apart from wisdom there is no principle. Essence and function are non-dual, like a pearl and its luster.
The ordinary person and the Buddha are fundamentally identical; the distinction between the ordinary and the sagely lies only in their realization.
How could the single mind differ? This is the intent of the present comprehensive explanation.
Because there is emptiness, there is existence; because there is existence, there is emptiness; because there is emptiness, there is not emptiness; because there is existence, there is not existence.
Regarding the statement "existence and emptiness" and so forth, which concludes the three preceding sections on the meaning by means of non-duality:

as for "existence and emptiness," the illusory existence of the conventional truth mentioned above is the very existence that is identical to emptiness; because its essence is not different from emptiness, it is said that "it does not exist.

This concludes the true nature of the conventional. As for "emptiness and existence," the absolute emptiness of the ultimate truth mentioned above is the very emptiness that is identical to existence.
Because its essence is not different from existence, it is called "not empty"; this concludes the preceding point regarding the conventional that is identical with the ultimate.
Since the object of observation is thus, the subject of observation is likewise; therefore, this serves as a general conclusion.

When the four attachments are extinguished—the emptiness of non-emptiness being empty yet uninterrupted, and the existence of non-existence being existent yet not eternal—then all four extremes vanish.
The hundred negations are thereby dispelled.

While the lower three [stages] of non-emptiness dispel emotional attachments, although the essence and function of the preceding object and wisdom are distinct, their nature is luminous and without difference—neither interrupted nor eternal, neither empty nor existent.
Regarding the various heterodox delusions and the proliferation of divergent calculations, although these were previously detailed...

Furthermore, because the Master fears that [the practitioner] might find it difficult to forget emotional attachments, he now sends forth a sweeping purification so that they may see the source of the mind.

As for the statement "not empty" and so forth, this reveals that the aforementioned true emptiness is the emptiness that is identical with existence; if it were divorced from existence, it would be a nihilistic emptiness (*uccheda-śūnyatā*).
Since it is not like that, it is said to be "neither severed nor non-existent" and so forth, which reveals that the aforementioned illusory existence is itself emptiness.
If existence were distinct from emptiness, it would follow that existence is permanent; since this is not the case, it is said to be "not permanent.

Regarding the four attachments: although they concern emptiness, existence, annihilation, and permanence, because one merely calculates a single aspect [of each], they are called the "four attachments.

Furthermore, for identity, difference, existence, and non-existence, there are four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) for each—namely, identity, non-identity, and so forth—as cited in sequence; whichever one of these is adhered to, it likewise constitutes an attachment.

Regarding the phrase "named the four attachments and called the hundred negations," the *Qixinlun ji* (Record of the Awakening of Faith) states: "This is explained in terms of the four positions—identity, difference, existence, and non-existence—and so forth.
Specifically, regarding 'one': it is not one, it is also one, it is neither one nor not one, and it is neither not-one nor not-not-one;

these constitute the four positions for 'one. The cases of 'difference' and so forth follow this pattern, together forming sixteen [positions]. Furthermore, there are ten [positions] each for the past, present, and future."
Sixty-four, plus another forty-eight for those already arisen and not yet arisen, together with the four fundamental [positions], total one hundred;

thus, they are all negated. Now, the intent of this commentary is simply that when discrimination does not arise and one remains in a state of tranquil oblivion, emotional attachments are naturally eliminated and errors and faults are thereby extinguished;
hence it is said: "Since the four attachments have perished, the hundred negations are thereby dispelled."
Is this not what is meant by the profound purport of Prajñā?

The two characters "Prajñā" at the beginning of the fourth section conclude the section on its profound and mysterious nature; these two characters directly refer to this very sutra while also encompassing the extensive sections as described above.
As for the principles and the wondrous, subtle purport of the single sutra’s exposition—whether regarding its objective realm (*viṣaya*) or its wisdom (*jñāna*)—the principle is as follows:
Because it reaches its ultimate limit here, it is said: "This is what is meant," or "This is it. These are merely expletives.
If one were to recount the events in full detail, the words would exceed two hundred thousand stanzas; yet if one extracts the essential core, the principle is exhausted in these fourteen lines.

If the two preceding sections [of the text] expound the *prajñā* that is expressed (*lakṣya*), while the current section addresses the expression itself (*lakṣaṇa*), then since this corresponds to the two types of *prajñā*—the *prajñā* of the true mark (*tathatā*) and the *prajñā* of contemplation—it follows that the present section concerns the *prajñā* of words (*vyañjana-prajñā*). The text is divided into three parts; first, it indicates the extensive and abbreviated versions.

Regarding the phrase "if one passes through" (*yadi kramate*) and so forth, this reveals the extensive version of that [scripture]. It refers to the exposition. Now, the extensive version of the *Prajñāpāramitā* consists of six [sections].
The total of one hundred fascicles is divided into eight sections, namely the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Large Version), the *Svalpaprajñāpāramitā* (Small Version), and so forth.

The subjects explained therein range from form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), comprising over eighty topical categories. Because this [text] now reveals their full extent, it is said to consist of two hundred thousand verses (*śloka*).
Regarding these "verses" (*śloka*), as explained in various commentaries, there are generally four types: first, the *anuṣṭubh* verse; [the others being the *gāthā*, *mātrā-vṛtta*, and *jāti-vṛtta*].
This does not distinguish between prose (*gadya*) and verse (*śloka*); rather, when the number of syllables reaches thirty-two, it constitutes one *śloka*.
Two *gāthās* are here called "recited verses" (*geya*) or "direct verses" (*sagāthaka*), because they directly praise the Dharma-gate through verse recitation.

Fourth is *geya*, here translated as "verses corresponding to prose," because they correspond to the preceding prose sections. Fourth is *udāna*, which means "accumulated. It refers to that which is accumulated.
Because the meaning of the Dharma is intended for recitation and retention, it is the first of the four [types of sūtras].

To summarize the following and reveal this abbreviated version is to "extract the pivot," which is a metaphor for its essential core—just as a door-pivot is central to a door. To unify the many into one is called the "essential principle" (*yāo-lǐ*), meaning the underlying *artha*.
This implies that if one were to fully traverse all phenomena and exhaustively explain the teaching methods, it would indeed be like the extensive sections.
If one were to select the grand framework from the six hundred fascicles and extract their essential meanings, this abbreviated version would already encompass them completely;
thus it is said that the principle is exhausted in these fourteen lines. Since ancient times, the texts of the scriptures have all taken seventeen characters as a single line;
therefore, this present scripture contains only fourteen lines.
Thus we know that the teachings which express the truth vary between being extensive or concise according to conditions.
Thus we know: the following two [sections] clarify the intent behind the extensiveness and conciseness. First, the extensiveness and conciseness arise from the capacity of the audience.

"Thus we know" refers back to the preceding text; "varies" (*cha*) means provisional or expedient. Since the text is called "teaching" because it expresses the true principle, it is termed "the teaching that expresses the truth. This is the meaning.
That which was described in the preceding text, whether extensively or concisely, is due solely to the fact that sentient beings possess either sharp or dull faculties.
Those with sharp faculties are suited to hear a concise exposition and thereby attain awakening, while those with dull faculties require an extensive exposition before they can understand.

This was not the Buddha’s original intent; hence the word "suddenly" (or "initially"). "Conditions" (pratyaya) refers to the conditions of the faculties—namely, the sharp and the dull—but here we are speaking only in terms of awakening.

To explain and distinguish between the sharp and the dull—if one were to distinguish them based on hearing and retention, the meaning would be the opposite of this; such is not the intent of the present commentary.
This is spoken in a transcendent manner: the fundamental nature is perfectly interfused and manifests all at once.

The principle that transcends words is eternally non-different from the "Principal" (the Master); because the True Reality that is expounded is the principal of the sutra, it is called the "Principal.
Because it is free from the characteristics of verbal expression, it is said to "transcend words.

Although the teaching that expresses it may be extensive or concise, the reality it expresses neither increases nor decreases. It is fundamentally perfect, harmonious, and manifests as equality. Therefore—

Regarding the passage beginning with "The nature of clouds is perfectly pervasive," etc.: The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* is truly what is called a lofty torch illuminating the dark thoroughfare and a swift vessel for crossing the sea of suffering.

Regarding "Prajñā" (at the bottom of the page), the threefold praise of its function is divided into two parts; first, the formal praise, where the phrase "is truly what is called" (*shí wèi*) specifically identifies [the sūtra].

The term "illumination" refers to radiance. As for "the dark thoroughfare," "thoroughfare" means a crossroads; "the dark thoroughfare" is a metaphor for the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), which are the causes of birth and death.

Next, it says "the sea of suffering," which refers to the reality of birth and death. Sentient beings within the triple world constantly dwell in these realms of suffering, drifting and sinking in birth and death;
there are none who fail to realize *bodhi* who do not do so because of these two obstructions. This is the name and essence of the two obstructions.

Extensive commentaries and exegeses exist in separate volumes; however, to provide a brief clarification: within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, the first [type of obscuration] is named the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*), whose essence consists of the root and secondary afflictions;

the second is named the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), whose essence is ignorance (*avidyā*). These are explained in detail according to their respective grammatical formations—*karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) and *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound)—as stated elsewhere.
Since the tenets of these systems differ, there is no need for extensive citation here. The *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra-vyākhyā* states: "The afflictive obscuration..."
The cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) obstructs the mind, so that the mind is not liberated; the afflictive hindrance obstructs wisdom (*prajñā*), so that wisdom is not liberated.

Since these are the very root of sentient beings' birth and death, and furthermore can obscure the principle and cognition of the nature of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma*), they are like a dark and narrow path where one will surely stumble and fall if one treads upon it, and thus cannot reach the destination ahead; therefore, this serves as a metaphor. As for the phrase "high torch," it refers to a tall torch.

The "torch" is a metaphor for *prajñā* (wisdom). This means that if one can rely on this scriptural passage to give rise to profound and wondrous wisdom, realizing that the mind is fundamentally quiescent and seeing that all phenomena are originally empty, then one will subsequently cultivate both compassion and wisdom, carrying oneself and others together.

When the dualities of acceptance and rejection are obliterated, and the conditions of favorability and adversity are transcended, the two obstacles are subtly eliminated and the three emptinesses may be realized—just like a torch.
The high radiance suddenly illuminates the dark alleys; how could it not arrive swiftly at the places mentioned before?

Therefore, it is said that [this wisdom] is truly the lofty torch that shines upon the dark alleys. Regarding "rescuing from suffering" and so forth: "rescue" means swift salvation. "Vessel" refers to a boat;

a swift vessel is also a metaphor for *prajñā*. "Suffering" refers to the two kinds of birth and death: *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative). This is because of the aforementioned...
Because they are induced by the two obstacles, the characteristics of the suffering of the two deaths are boundless, comparable to the ocean.

Thus, the three realms are unstable and there is nothing that is not suffering; yet sentient beings, lacking wisdom, delusively reckon them to be happiness. When observed with true knowledge, how could there be anything pleasurable?
Therefore, our Great Sage, through the power of his compassion and vows, has specifically expounded this scripture to rescue and deliver [beings].
Sentient beings are thus enabled to board the wisdom-vessel of Prajñāpāramitā and swiftly cross the turbulent sea of suffering; therefore, the subsequent scripture states:
"Practicing profound Prajñā, one illuminates the emptiness of the five aggregates and transcends all suffering," and so forth.
In saving sentient beings and guiding those who are deluded, nothing surpasses this [sūtra].
"Saving beings" refers to the two [aspects of] rescue and reception; "guiding" refers to leading. "Beings" refers to the capacities of sentient beings, and "delusion" refers to confusion.
This clearly demonstrates that this single sūtra is decisively able to lead the deluded, rescuing and receiving their capacities so that they may leave behind the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
If one treads the dark alleys upon the level and luminous path of wisdom, then even the high precipice of Nirvana can be ascended;
how could one doubt crossing the gentle ripples of birth and death? I address this to future students: reflect upon it and put it into practice.

This concludes the preceding meaning, which previously lamented the illumination of the dark alleys and the salvation from the sea of suffering; thus, it is now said that [the teaching] provides succor.
Among all things that lead the deluded astray, none is more so than this.
Thus, Prajñā takes spiritual discernment as its essence, while the Pāramitās take reaching the other shore as their function;
the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* reveals the essential subtleties of the mind, and the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* penetrates through the verbal teachings.
Thus, the following two sections briefly outline the titles of the sutras. First, regarding the formal exposition of "Prajñā" and so forth:

*Prajñā* is translated here as "wisdom. "Spirit" (*shen*) refers to that which cannot be fathomed; "mirror" (*jian*) refers to the capacity for clear reflection. Its essence (*ti*) is its very nature (*xing*).

The intent is to reveal that although this wisdom is unfathomable, its nature is constantly reflective and illuminating; therefore, it is said that its essence consists of the spirit-mirror. *Pāramitā*...
The phrase "honey and so forth" cites both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms; it reveals that this wisdom possesses the functional capacity to depart from this [shore] and reach that [shore].
Thus, the meaning of "departing and reaching" is explained as follows in the section on the commentary of the title. Regarding "the heart being manifest and so forth":

because the human heart is the essential, vital, subtle, and wondrous locus to which the entire body returns, it serves as a metaphor for this *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, which is the brief version of that extensive treatise.
This is the essential point. Furthermore, as explained below regarding the interpretation of the sūtra, the "equal" (等) refers to the simultaneous manifestation of both the dharma and the metaphor.
Because the sūtra can uphold meaning, it is likened to a thread that can string flowers so they do not scatter or be lost;
thus, this sūtra consists of the verbal teachings that uphold principles and meanings, which is why it is called a "sūtra" (經), signifying that which "strings together" (貫穿) and so forth.
Because the title expresses its essential meaning by proceeding from the Dharma to the metaphor, it is called the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.
From the word "Dharma" downward, the second section provides a summary: "Dharma" refers to that which is illustrated, namely *prajñā* and so forth;

the word "heart" (*hṛdaya*) is that which does the illustrating, meaning the expressive term, namely the single character "sūtra"; and "essential meaning" (*artha*) refers to that which is expressed, namely the ultimate intent of the aforementioned Dharma and metaphor.
Since these [terms]—the "equal" (etc.)—combine the dharma, the metaphor, the capacity, and the object to form the title of this sutra, it is summarized by saying:
"from the dharma, proceeding toward the metaphor, etc.

To explain this sutra, there is a fivefold analysis: first, the arising of the teaching; second, its inclusion within the Pitakas; third, its essential purport; fourth, the explanation of the title; and fifth, [the commentary on the text].
Fifth, the explanation of the text.
Regarding the upcoming commentary on the latter two sections, there is a twofold analysis of the sutra text: first, the listing of the chapters; second, the five gates, etc.

Of these, the former three provide a preliminary judgment, while the latter two explain the sutra text. Furthermore, there is a systematic sequence to the arising of these five gates. Why is this? For when the Sages speak...

Since every teaching must have its causes and conditions, the reasons for the emergence of the teachings are distinguished; once the teachings have emerged, they do not exceed the Three Piṭakas, and thus they are subsumed within the Abhidharma Piṭaka.

Although one knows how the general purport of what is subsumed is, the fundamental intent is nevertheless shown. Having already understood the general purport, the titles of the sūtras must be clarified;
therefore, it is said that "the titles are explained. Although the titles are manifest, one has not yet understood how to enter the sūtra; therefore, the text itself must be interpreted.

Regarding the initial emergence of the teaching, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is said that even Sumeru, the King of Mountains, cannot be shaken without causes and conditions, nor by minor causes and conditions.
In the first of the five sections of the subsequent commentary, the first part cites a metaphor from the treatise; this treatise is [the work of] Nāgārjuna.
The Bodhisattva Shu composed this commentary on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Now, in order to explain the *Prajñā*, he specifically cites Mount Sumeru and other examples.
In Sanskrit, it is called Sumeru; translated [into Chinese], it means "Wondrously High" (*Miaogao*). It is composed of four precious substances, hence "Wondrous";
it emerges eighty thousand *yojanas* from the water, hence "High. Because it is the most honored among all mountains, it is called "King. It is not that there are none equal to it.
This, conversely, reveals that because that mountain possesses causes and conditions—and indeed many causes and conditions—it is only through them that it can be made to tremble.

For this mountain to tremble, there must be a superior condition (*viśiṣṭa-pratyaya*), namely, the Buddhas manifesting their birth and achieving enlightenment through the eight phases (*aṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*).
This is fully detailed in that treatise. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "There has never been a single dharma that does not arise from causes and conditions."
The arising of the Prajñā teachings is likewise so because they possess many causes and conditions.
Regarding the three points concerning the causes and conditions for the emergence of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other scriptures: first, it is marked by the fact that they possess many conditions.

As for the phrase "the Prajñā teachings and so forth," the teachings of Prajñā revealed in those treatises must arise by possessing the necessary conditions; like Mount Sumeru, they do not shake without conditions.
Therefore, it is said, "it is also thus," and so forth.
First, it is because he wishes to destroy the various false views of the non-Buddhists; second, because he wishes to turn back those of the two vehicles and cause them to enter the Mahāyāna;

third, because he wishes to prevent lesser bodhisattvas from becoming confused regarding emptiness; and fourth, because he wishes to cause them to realize the Middle Way within the two truths and give rise to right view.
First, to manifest the Buddha’s supreme virtues so that pure faith may arise; second, to cause the aspiration for great bodhicitta to be generated;

third, to cause the cultivation of the profound and vast practices of a bodhisattva; fourth, to cause all heavy obstacles to be severed; fifth, to cause the fruits of bodhi and nirvāṇa to be attained;
sixth, to cause these teachings to flow down to future generations to benefit sentient beings.

First, the first two [sections] briefly reveal ten meanings; yet these ten meanings do not depart from persons (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*), understanding (*adhimukti*) and practice (*pratipatti*), cause (*hetu*) and fruit (*phala*), and compassion (*karuṇā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding self-cultivation and transforming others: the first three concern persons, while the remainder are all phenomena.

Furthermore, the fourth and fifth belong to understanding, while the sixth through the eighth belong to practice. Moreover, the first eight are causes, while the ninth corresponds to the fruit. Furthermore, the first nine...
This wisdom is followed by one [aspect] which is compassion; furthermore, from the fourth to the ninth are for one’s own practice, while the remainder are for the transformation of others.
This applies not only to the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras but extends to other scriptures as well, because all require the possession of these various causes and conditions.

Now, following this classification, they are collectively grouped into four: first, those that break the heterodox attachments of non-Buddhists and the like, which are the mental activities [of such beings].
Because they cultivate only false causes outside of the principle, they are called "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika); because their views do not manifest correct understanding, they are called "false views.

However, these non-Buddhist false views do not depart from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; based upon these, the sixty-two views and so forth arise, as explained extensively in other volumes.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Deeply attached to false dharmas, they cling to them firmly and cannot relinquish them; if they were to know emptiness and stillness..."
Because all views naturally perish, it is called "shattering. The "Two Vehicles" refers to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;

these two classes of persons dwell only in the "transformed city" (the provisional stage) rather than ascending to the "Jeweled Place" (the ultimate goal). They are capable only of self-benefit and do not aspire to transform others.

If they hear that both [subject and object] are empty, their sense of self and other will necessarily vanish; they will suddenly turn back from the narrow path and immediately advance upon the Great Highway. Therefore, it is said: "desiring to turn back."
Those of the two vehicles and lesser bodhisattvas refer to those at the stage of the ten levels of faith and the stage of application (*prayoga*).
Regarding the ten levels of faith, they have not yet understood the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), as illustrated by the three doubts cited from the *Ratnagotravibhāga*.

As for the stage of application, conceptualization has not yet been eliminated; they take emptiness as something to be attained. As the verse says: "Because there is something to be attained, it is not the true dwelling. Only... [the true dwelling].

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is generally categorized as delusion by those following conventional examples and thus disparaged as "small" (*hīna*). However, if one hears the Prajñāpāramitā, which dissolves and washes away all distinctions between right and wrong, one may enter the stage of the Three Worthies (*triyāna-śaikṣa*) and immediately ascend to the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*);
therefore, it is said that this causes the "small" not to be deluded. Fourth, regarding the phrase "causing the two lower [stages] to cause the causal practices to accomplish the Two Truths," etc.:

to realize the True (*tattva*) is precisely to know the Conventional (*saṃvṛti*), and to know the Conventional is precisely to realize the True; since the True and the Conventional are without distinction, there is only...
The single Middle Way alone is called Right View, as the Sūtra says: "Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form.

Since emptiness and form are themselves the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional, their mutual identity reveals the Middle Way. Regarding the revelation of the Buddha’s virtues and so forth:
the Buddha’s virtues are immeasurable, yet they are subsumed within four meanings, namely, permanence, bliss, self, and purity. This is the Perfect Enlightenment.
The Commentary states: "Eternity, bliss, self, and purity are the virtues of the Buddha. Although all phenomena are empty, the Buddha’s virtues do not deviate from this [reality].
One who, through patient acceptance, joy, and pure faith, gives rise to the Bodhicitta without doubt—this essence of Bodhicitta consists of compassion, wisdom, and the vow.
Since the wondrous, ultimate reality of true emptiness is identical for both oneself and others, and since others have long been lost in delusion, one employs compassion to transform them."
Since one has not yet personally realized this, one must seek it upward through wisdom; if the essential commitment were lacking, how could the essence of the three minds be accomplished?
From this point, the practice of the profound and vast conduct arises. Now, the bodhisattva practices are generally of two kinds:

first, those that follow signs (*nimitta*), and second, those that are free from signs. Because they are free from signs, they are tranquil and without attainment; therefore, they are called "profound."
That is, one cultivates the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) by relying on the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*);

because it follows [the nature of] phenomena, and because the myriad practices are fully cultivated, it is called "extensive," which refers to cultivating the practice of *vipaśyanā* (insight) by relying on the gate of arising and ceasing. These two practices support one another and must not be viewed in isolation.
As stated in the *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra*: "Therefore, although one exerts oneself in cultivation, from beginning to end there is no sign, so as to sever the heavy obstacles," and so forth.

The obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) are precisely the afflictive (*kleśa*) and cognitive (*jñeya*) obstructions, as briefly explained above. Because they weigh down sentient beings, causing them to sink forever into the ocean of suffering, they are called "heavy.

If one clarifies the principle of emptiness, how could these two obstructions remain? The *Vajra Commentary* states: "If the two types of grasping are eliminated, the two obstructions will accordingly be severed.

One should understand that the intent of this present sutra, being of the same category, follows the same principle. However, in order to cultivate the path, correct understanding must take precedence.
Initially, when this understanding manifests, it takes faith as its foundation. Once faith and understanding are complete, one must give rise to the three minds.
When faith and understanding arise, the mind is intent upon practice; once wondrous practice is perfected, the afflictions and obstacles naturally perish.

This sequence of five conditions should logically be thus. The nine [faculties] cause the lower three fetters to be abandoned; the fruit of virtue is fulfilled, wherein Bodhi is the fruit of wisdom and Nirvāṇa is the fruit of cessation.
Regarding the fruits of severance, as the sutra states: "By relying on prajñā, one attains bodhi, nirvāṇa, and so forth.

As for the last four of the ten streams, they are intended to benefit future generations; here, "generations" (dài) refers to successive eras. Now, when discussing emptiness and dispelling attachments, the underlying intent lies in benefiting living beings;
how could it be merely for the sake of a single period? It must be transmitted through successive kalpas. For this reason, the exhortations and entrustments in that treatise are exceedingly earnest.

I entrust this to future worthies: do not grow weary in upholding and expounding it. The ten conditions mentioned above are condensed into four: first, the intent of the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra is to shatter attachments;
once the sentiments of attachment are dispelled, one must practice the causal conduct. Once that practice is complete, the fruit of realization is attained.
Having personally realized the fruit, one then teaches and transforms others. The arising of the *Prajñāpāramitā* is solely for this purpose.
To explain briefly: these ten [topics] fully encompass the intent of that [treatise] so as to make known the emergence of the teaching.
Regarding the phrase "briefly explained," the three subsequent points summarize the intent to return to the fundamental source. The meaning of "briefly explained" and so forth is this:
since that treatise mostly concerns itself with nothing other than these ten great chapters, and since the present sutra is likewise so, it is said "to make known the emergence of the teaching."
Regarding inclusion within the second treasury: among the three treasuries, it is included in the Sūtra-piṭaka; among the two treasuries, it is subsumed under the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Within these two [categories], the first clarifies inclusion within the treasuries. As for the "three treasuries," they are the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma; in Sanskrit, this is called *piṭaka*.

*Sūtra* is translated here as *qìjīng* (Scripture of Accordance); it refers to a scripture that accords with both principle (*lǐ*) and capacity (*jī*). It is called a "Scripture of Accordance" (*qìjīng*) to distinguish it from the Vinaya and Abhidharma;

thus, it is said to be subsumed within the *Qìjīng-zàng* (Sūtra-piṭaka). This is fully explained in works such as the records and commentaries on the *Yuánjué jīng* (Complete Enlightenment Sūtra) and the *Qǐxìn lùn* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith).

Regarding the two piṭakas, these refer to the Śrāvaka and Bodhisattva [piṭakas]. The three piṭakas are categorized by way of the Dharma, while the two piṭakas are categorized by way of the person. Based on the above three...

The "Piṭaka of the Śrāvakas" refers to that which reveals the principles, practices, and fruits of the Hīnayāna; the "Piṭaka of the Bodhisattvas" refers to that which reveals the principles, practices, and fruits of the Mahāyāna.
Since this sutra states that bodhisattvas attain ultimate nirvāṇa, it is known not to belong to the Hīnayāna, and therefore it is subsumed within the Piṭaka of the Bodhisattvas.
Within the provisional and real teachings, this is subsumed under the real teaching.

Although the provisional and real teachings below clarify the inclusion of the teachings, since the language of "Great Mahāyāna" in the present sutra applies universally to both the provisional and the real, it is subsumed under the real teaching.
As the subsequent sutra states: "Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form. This reveals the nature of form.

Regarding the statement that emptiness is non-dual, unique, and the single true reality, and further that both those on the path of cause and those who have attained the fruit realize ultimate Bodhi and Nirvana—this should be understood as being subsumed under the "True Teaching" (*nītārtha*), for it is not provisional (*neyārtha*).

Question: According to Xianshou’s Five Teachings Classification (*Wujiao Zhang*), which exhausts the meaning of all scriptures, the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras discuss the principle of emptiness and thus belong to the Initial Teaching (*shijiao*).
Since the Initial Teaching is categorized as provisional, why do you say it is subsumed under the True Teaching? Answer: If one considers...

The separate treatises pertain strictly to the Initial Teaching (śikṣā), but here we rely on the general meaning and thus include it within the Real Teaching. The *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* states:

"There are both general and specific [meanings]; this is according to the explicit teaching. Although this was briefly explained when previously clarifying the objective realm (*viṣaya*), one should reflect upon this:
while this is the "reality" of the provisional and real teachings, it is not the ultimate reality. May students contemplate this.
Regarding the third point, the "tenet" (*siddhānta*) is that which is expressed by speech, and the "orientation" (*gati*) is the destination toward which the tenet tends.
Among these three [terms], two are explained first: the name is explained in general. "Speech" refers to linguistic expression; "expressed" means to represent or indicate.

"Tenet" (*siddhānta*)—where *siddha* means "venerated" or "esteemed," and *anta* means "destination" or "tendency"—all signify the sense of "moving toward. Thus, speech is the means of expression (*vyañjaka*), while the tenet is the object expressed (*vyaṅgya*). Speech is the agent of expression.

The statement "that which is expressed by words" refers to the fact that whatever is venerated must have a specific object toward which it is directed; hence the phrase "that which is expressed by speech," and so forth.

Now, first generally and then specifically, the general principle takes the three types of *prajñā* as its core: first, the *lakṣaṇa-prajñā* (wisdom of characteristics), which refers to the true reality (*tattva*) that is the object of contemplation.
The two natures refer to the contemplation that observes; the sublime wisdom that is capable of observing; and the three syllables, which refer to the teachings that express the former two.
Since nothing exceeds these three, they are taken as the core tenet (*zong*).

Now, first, regarding the second part [of the introduction], there is a separate explanation of the meaning in two sections: first, a general explanation of the core tenet alone; then, the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* speaks of *prajñā*.

If there are five kinds [of prajñā], the first three are as explained in the commentary; the fourth, "prajñā associated with wisdom," refers to the simultaneous occurrence of the mental king (citta-rāja) and its mental factors (caitta), which constitute the five attendants of prajñā.
This is simultaneous with wisdom. The fifth, "prajñā of the five aggregates," refers to the simultaneous occurrence of the five aggregates with wisdom.

Since the first three are the primary [forms], they are employed here. Regarding the "one true mark" (eka-lakṣaṇa), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "From the very beginning, it is neither born nor extinguished."
First, "true reality" (bhūtalakṣaṇa) refers to that which is taken as the object of contemplation.

Second, "contemplative illumination" means that since there is an object that is illuminated, there must necessarily be the wisdom that illuminates it; this illuminating function is called the "contemplative wisdom" (prajñā).
Third, "words and letters" refers to the verbal teachings that can express the preceding two [realities and wisdom]. Thus, these constitute the contemplator and the...
Since the consideration of both the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*) constitutes the primary subject matter of speech, it is said that they do not transcend [the nature of] equality.
Furthermore, both the true reality (*dharmatā*) and written words (*akṣara*) are called *prajñā*: the true reality can give rise to wisdom, and written words can express wisdom;
therefore, both are named *prajñā*. Moreover, the *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra* states: "The emptiness of the nature of written words is itself *prajñā*."

There are also three further distinctions: first, the pair of teaching and meaning, where the text of the teaching is taken as the primary focus (*mūla*) and the underlying meaning as the goal (*prayojana*);
second, the pair of object and wisdom, where the realm of true emptiness is taken as the primary focus and contemplative wisdom as the goal;
third, the pair of cause and fruit, where the causal practices for enlightenment are taken as the primary focus and the resultant virtues of enlightenment as the goal.

Regarding "the distinction, as well as the lower two distinctions, together with the fundamental tenet (*zongqu*), the one teaching-meaning (*jiaoyi*), etc.": this refers to taking the first three divisions of Prajñā collectively as the fundamental tenet.
"Meaning" (*yi*) refers to that which is explained—the latter two types of Prajñā; "teaching" (*jiao*) refers to that which explains—the *prajñā* of words and letters.
Now, the "tenet" (*zong*) is the intended purport of the explanatory teachings and words, while the "meaning" (*yi*) is the reality of the objects and wisdom being explained.
Regarding "the two: object and wisdom," this distinguishes the fundamental tenets (*siddhānta*) concerning the two dharmas of the object and wisdom as explained above.
Now, as for the true object as the fundamental tenet: the intention is that wisdom is generated from the object, and because the object is illuminated by wisdom, wisdom is taken as the goal (*gati*).
Regarding "the three: cause and fruit": Bodhi is the fruit, and causal practice is wisdom; thus, [wisdom] is that which realizes [the fruit].
The practice that serves as the cause for bodhi takes the wisdom capable of illumination mentioned previously as its primary thesis (*pakṣa*).
Within this causal context, the practitioner cultivates this wisdom because they intend to realize the fruit of bodhi; thus, the qualities of the fruit serve as the goal (*uddeśa*).

Regarding these three pairs, the first pertains to understanding (*adhimukti*), the second to practice (*caryā*), and the third to realization (*sākṣātkriyā*); these constitute the sequence of understanding, practice, and realization.
Realizing the Three [Natures] is precisely the central purport of this single sūtra.
[Sūtra] *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, Chapter Four.

Regarding the explanation of the title, there are also three pairs; first, according to the meaning of the Initial Teaching, they are divided into two: namely, *prajñā* (wisdom) and *hṛdaya* (heart/essence) are that which is...
Regarding the meaning of "explaining" (*quan*), the single character "sūtra" (*jing*) refers to the teaching that is capable of explaining.

Among the four [sections], the commentary (*shu*) has three parts: first, citing the chapter; second, the formal explanation of the title of the sūtra; and third, within the first [of these], there are two [subdivisions].

The first [subdivision] specifically points to the examples of the teaching and its meaning found previously in the section on the "doctrinal intent" (*zongqu*); therefore, it now says "also. The phrase "teaching and meaning, etc. clarifies this.

Although the title of the sutra consists of eight characters, taken as a whole, they do not deviate from the two categories of doctrine (teaching) and meaning (significance). Prajñā is the mind of the Dharma, which is a metaphor;
thus, both the metaphor and the Dharma belong to the category of the "meaning" (*sūtrārtha*) that is explained.
The word "sūtra" (經) belongs to the teaching that functions as the expressive means (*vyañjana*).
It is a sūtra that expresses the *prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya*, and its name is established based on its meaning.

That is to say, it expresses the two [aspects] below, while generally manifesting the establishment of the name as the expressive means for the meanings below, as explained previously regarding "based on the meaning" and so forth.
The title of a single sutra is established based on the meaning of the dharma and the analogy that are expressed;
therefore, it is titled "Prajñā" and so forth.

Second, within the meaning of what is expressed, there are two divisions: the dharma and the analogy. That is to say, "Prajñā" and so forth refer to the dharma that is expressed, while "citta" [refers to the analogy].
The character "one" (之) refers to the metaphor being cited.

Regarding the second [section], the first part specifically points to both the dharma and the metaphor; this excludes the character "sūtra" (經) and divides the two—dharma and metaphor—solely within the seven characters that constitute the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
This is precisely the wondrous meaning of the essential core unified within Prajñā; furthermore, the human mind is the sovereign, the vital essence, and the fundamental basis of unification.

Regarding the phrase "precisely within Prajñā" and the following two sections, which apply the Dharma to the analogy: first, it indicates the Dharma. "Precisely within Prajñā" is a general [statement].

"Pointing to the Essentials of the Extensive Sections" (referring to the lower part) reveals that this present abbreviated version is the comprehensive essential path, the center, the middle, and the correct.

By means of this abbreviated version, the dharma-gates it elucidates comprehensively encompass the essential paths, the central and correct, and the subtle and wondrous meanings within the six hundred fascicles of the extensive sections.
Furthermore, "as for people" below points to a metaphor; just as within a human body, although...

There are five treasuries (*pañca-kośa*); yet, as for that which clearly and brilliantly masters the essential path and governs the ultimate source, it is solely the treasury of the mind (*citta-kośa*).
Therefore, it is said to be the master and the essential. While the four other treasuries of the body serve as metaphors for the extensive sections, the treasury of the mind governs the essentials;
this brief text uses them as analogies for comparison.
Third, within the aforementioned dharma, the essence (*tī*) and function (*yòng*) are divided into two; that is, *prajñā* is the essence, which here is translated as "wisdom" (*zhìhuì*).

Of the three [sections], the first two explain the essence. Furthermore, excluding the single character "mind" (*xīn*), one distinguishes the two—essence and function—solely based on the six characters within the metaphorical dharma.
The text has two parts: first, the direct indication of the essence and the translation of the name, according to the *Kanding ji*.

To explain: "na" (那) is the opposite of "knowledge" (智), which belongs to the fruit; "ruo" (若) is the opposite of "wisdom" (慧), which belongs to the cause. Since this present discussion treats them collectively, it translates them as "wisdom-knowledge" (智慧).
This refers to the divine awakening to profound mysteries and the subtle realization of the true source.
Regarding "the divine descends" and so forth, which explicitly reveals the essence of wisdom: "awakening" (*wu*) refers to enlightenment.

This reveals that the essence of this unfathomable wisdom is its fundamental awakening (*benjue*), which is naturally profound, mysterious, and abstruse. Regarding "wondrous realization" (*miaozheng*) and so forth:

"realization" (*zheng*) carries the meaning of a dark, mystical resonance; it means that this essence of wisdom is subtly and wondrously in resonance with the source of true emptiness (*zhenshūng*). As for...
Because this is the wisdom of principle (*li*), it is called "wondrously realizing the source of the mind.
*Pāramitā* is its function; here it is translated as "reaching the other shore" (*dào bǐ àn*).
Regarding the two explanations for *pāramitā*, the first indicates the function and translates the name: "reaching the other shore" is established by the *Kanding* (Determination of the Canon).
The *Record* states: "Birth and death are the 'this shore' because sentient beings dwell there; afflictions are the 'middle current' because they are the most difficult to cross;
and nirvana is the 'other shore' because all Buddhas abide there—thus, the other shore is used as a metaphor for nirvana.
Since nirvana is that which is reached and wisdom is that which reaches it, the character 'to reach' (dào) applies to both the agent and the object."
It is precisely because of this wondrous wisdom that one overturns the faults of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and reaches the limit of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
it is named as such because it distinguishes itself from the wisdom that fails to reach the other shore.

The phrase "precisely because of this" and below correctly reveals the function of wisdom. Regarding "the faults of birth-and-death" and so forth: indeed, sentient beings are unable to realize [this].
That which is true emptiness takes the two kinds of birth and death—fragmentary and transformative—as its fundamental affliction.
If wondrous wisdom arises, one realizes that all phenomena are empty, and even this "sickness" of emptiness is itself empty.
Being carefree and without dependence, how could there be this shore of birth and death? How could one not leave the other shore of nirvana? True emptiness is precisely nirvana. Since...
Since it is by means of this that one can overturn birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and attain *nirvāṇa*, how could it not be employed? Thus, it is said, "by virtue of this wondrous wisdom," and so forth.

As for the phrase "distinguishing those who do not reach [it]": the shallow wisdom of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) merely clarifies that the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) is the cause of birth-and-death and does not transcend the triple world;
this is not worth discussing. Although the wisdom of the Two Vehicles is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*), it only realizes a partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*).
However, although those who have lost the stage of *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented death) and Bodhisattvas of the ten stages possess a portion of *pariṇāmi-kāya* (transformative death),

these two types of persons have not yet been called those who have ultimately attained the wisdom that reaches the other shore. Now, this wondrous wisdom understands the principle of the two emptinesses,

practices the path of the two emptinesses, severs the delusions of the two obstacles, leaves behind the suffering of the two deaths, realizes the bliss of the two virtues, and dwells securely in sublime awakening.
Abiding in nirvāṇa is alone termed the wisdom that has ultimately reached the other shore; this is because "the other shore" is defined here in terms of the ultimate fruit.
Thus, it is said that those who have not reached it are excluded, as their excellence and inferiority differ; therefore, they must be distinguished and differentiated.
This means that because the essence is itself the function, it serves as the analogy for the phenomena (*dharma*) and the teaching for the meaning (*artha*); thus, this name is established.

Regarding the phrase "the essence" and below: the three [sections] consisting of sixfold explanations conclude by returning to the preceding text, as they have already provided a comprehensive understanding of the single title through the three aspects of teaching, meaning, and so forth.
Therefore, the current summary of the preceding three [sections] is subsumed under the sixfold explanations. The phrase "the essence is itself the function" concludes the third [section].
It also reveals that this wondrous wisdom takes the essence of total spiritual awakening as its substance and accomplishes the function of being free from faults;
therefore, it says "is" (*ji*). Regarding "the dharma of the metaphor," this concludes the second [section]. "Dharma" refers to *prajñā*, while "metaphor" refers to the word "mind";

because the metaphor is distinguished from the dharma, it says "of. Regarding "the teaching of the meaning," this concludes the first [section]. The dharma and the metaphor belong to the objective realm (*ālambana*).
The characters of the sūtra’s words are the "expressive teaching" (*vācaka-śāsana*), distinguished as the means of expression rather than the object expressed; thus they are also called "words.
As for the names: the first is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound), while the other two are *tatpuruṣa* (determinative compounds).

Therefore, the compilers of the sūtra established the title of this single scripture by combining the three aforementioned categories—teaching, meaning, and so forth—naming it the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.
